lessons.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
lessons.summary: Find out why some reactions warm their surroundings and others cool them, draw and read reaction profiles, and calculate energy changes from bond energies.
objectives: I can describe exothermic and endothermic reactions in terms of energy transfer to or from the surroundings.
I can give everyday and laboratory examples of each type of reaction.
I can draw and interpret reaction profiles, including activation energy.
I can explain energy changes in terms of bonds broken and bonds made.
I can calculate the overall energy change of a reaction using bond energies (Higher).

activities.title: Energy in and energy out
activities.content:
## Energy is conserved

When a chemical reaction happens, energy is never created or destroyed. It is only **transferred** between the reacting chemicals and their **surroundings** (the air, the beaker, the water the chemicals are dissolved in, your hand).

### Exothermic reactions

An **exothermic** reaction **transfers energy to the surroundings**, usually as heat. The surroundings get **warmer**, so a thermometer in the reaction mixture shows a **rise** in temperature.

Examples:
- **Combustion** (burning fuels)
- **Neutralisation** of an acid by an alkali
- Many **oxidation** reactions, such as metals reacting with acid
- Hand warmers and self-heating cans

### Endothermic reactions

An **endothermic** reaction **takes in energy from the surroundings**. The surroundings get **cooler**, so the thermometer reading **falls**.

Examples:
- **Thermal decomposition**, such as heating calcium carbonate
- Citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate (used in sherbet)
- Instant cold packs for sports injuries

A quick way to remember: **exo** = **exit**, energy goes out; **endo** = **enter**, energy goes in.

activities.title: Worked example: measuring a temperature change
activities.content:
**A student adds 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 19 °C to 27 °C. What type of reaction is this?**

The temperature of the mixture **rose by 8 °C**. Energy was transferred **to** the solution (the surroundings of the reacting ions), so this neutralisation is **exothermic**.

**Why use a polystyrene cup with a lid?**

Polystyrene is a good insulator, so less energy escapes to the air. The lid cuts down losses from the surface. Both make the measured temperature change closer to the true value.

**A second experiment:** sherbet powder is stirred into water and the temperature falls from 20 °C to 15 °C. A fall of 5 °C means energy was taken **in** from the water, so this reaction is **endothermic**.

**Watch out:** the temperature change tells you the direction of energy transfer, but the reaction itself is not "hot" or "cold". The thermometer measures the surroundings.

question.text: Which of the following are exothermic changes? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Exothermic reactions release energy and warm their surroundings.
question.explanation: Burning methane and neutralisation both release energy to the surroundings. Thermal decomposition and cold packs take energy in, so they are endothermic.

options.text: burning methane in a gas hob
sodium hydroxide neutralising sulfuric acid
heating copper carbonate until it decomposes
options.feedback: Thermal decomposition needs a continuous supply of energy, so it is endothermic.

options.text: an instant cold pack being activated
options.feedback: The pack gets cold because the reaction takes energy in from the surroundings.

activities.title: Reaction profiles
activities.content:
## Drawing the energy change

A **reaction profile** is a graph showing the energy of the chemicals as a reaction progresses. Energy is on the vertical axis; "progress of reaction" is on the horizontal axis.

### Exothermic profile

The **products are lower** than the reactants. The difference in height is the **energy released**.

```
energy
  |   reactants ___
  |              \__ hump __
  |                          \
  |                           \___ products
  |________________________________ progress
```

### Endothermic profile

The **products are higher** than the reactants. The difference is the **energy absorbed**.

```
energy
  |                      ___ products
  |             __ hump /
  |            /
  | reactants_/
  |________________________________ progress
```

### Activation energy

In both profiles there is a hump. Particles must collide with at least this much energy before a reaction can start. The height from the reactants up to the top of the hump is the **activation energy**. It is the minimum energy needed to break the first bonds and get things going.

This is why a match is needed to light a candle: the wax and oxygen need a push over the hump, even though the overall reaction gives out lots of energy.

A **catalyst** provides a different route with a **lower activation energy**, so the hump is smaller, but the start and end levels stay exactly the same.

activities.title: Worked example: reading a reaction profile
activities.content:
**A reaction profile shows reactants at 120 kJ, the peak of the hump at 200 kJ, and products at 50 kJ. Describe the reaction.**

**Step 1: exothermic or endothermic?**

Products (50 kJ) are **lower** than reactants (120 kJ), so energy is released. The reaction is **exothermic**.

**Step 2: overall energy change**

50 − 120 = **−70 kJ**. The negative sign shows energy leaving the reacting chemicals.

**Step 3: activation energy**

From reactants up to the peak: 200 − 120 = **80 kJ**.

**Step 4: with a catalyst**

If a catalyst lowers the peak to 160 kJ, the activation energy becomes 160 − 120 = 40 kJ. The overall energy change is still −70 kJ, because the catalyst does not change the reactants or products.

**Tip:** activation energy is always measured from the **reactants**, never from the products.

question.text: On a reaction profile the reactants are at 300 kJ, the top of the activation energy hump is at 450 kJ and the products are at 380 kJ. Calculate the activation energy in kJ.
question.hint: Activation energy is measured from the reactants up to the peak.
question.explanation: 450 − 300 = 150 kJ. (The reaction is endothermic because the products are higher than the reactants, but that does not change how the activation energy is measured.)

question.text: A catalyst is added to an exothermic reaction. Which statement about the reaction profile is correct?
question.hint: A catalyst offers an easier route, but the chemicals at the start and end are the same.
question.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy (the hump) but does not change the energy of the reactants or products, so the overall energy change stays the same.

options.text: The activation energy is lower, but the overall energy change is unchanged.
The products end up at a lower energy level, so more energy is released.
options.feedback: The products are the same chemicals, so their energy is unchanged.

options.text: The reaction becomes endothermic.
The activation energy increases so the reaction is slower.
options.feedback: Catalysts lower the activation energy and speed reactions up.

activities.title: Bonds broken and bonds made
activities.content:
## Where the energy actually comes from

Every reaction involves two steps at the level of atoms:

1. **Breaking** the bonds in the reactants. This **needs** energy, so bond breaking is **endothermic**.
2. **Making** the new bonds in the products. This **releases** energy, so bond making is **exothermic**.

The overall energy change is the balance between the two.

- If the energy **released** when new bonds form is **greater** than the energy needed to break the old ones, the reaction is **exothermic** overall.
- If **more** energy is needed to break bonds than is released when new ones form, the reaction is **endothermic** overall.

### Bond energy (Higher)

Each type of bond has a **bond energy**: the energy needed to break one mole of that bond, in kJ/mol. The same amount is released when the bond is made.

| Bond | Bond energy (kJ/mol) |
|---|---|
| H–H | 436 |
| Cl–Cl | 242 |
| H–Cl | 431 |
| O=O | 498 |
| O–H | 464 |

### The formula

**energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds**

or, more simply, **bonds broken − bonds made**.

A **negative** answer means exothermic; a **positive** answer means endothermic.

activities.title: Worked example: bond energy calculation
activities.content:
**Calculate the energy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl using the bond energies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.**

**Step 1: bonds broken (reactants)**

| Bond | Number | Energy |
|---|---|---|
| H–H | 1 | 436 |
| Cl–Cl | 1 | 242 |

Total to break = 436 + 242 = **678 kJ**

**Step 2: bonds made (products)**

2HCl means **two** H–Cl bonds: 2 × 431 = **862 kJ** released.

**Step 3: energy change**

broken − made = 678 − 862 = **−184 kJ/mol**

The answer is negative, so the reaction is **exothermic**. More energy was released making the two strong H–Cl bonds than was needed to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds.

**The most common mistake:** forgetting to multiply by the number in front of the formula. 2HCl has two bonds, not one. Always draw or count every bond before adding up.

question.text: Higher tier. Calculate the energy change, in kJ/mol, for the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Bond energies: H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. Give a negative answer if the reaction is exothermic.
question.hint: Break two H–H bonds and one O=O bond. Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, and there are two water molecules.
question.explanation: Broken: (2 × 436) + 498 = 1370 kJ. Made: 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ. Change = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ/mol, exothermic.

metadata.blanksText: Breaking bonds is an ___ process because energy must be supplied. Making bonds is an ___ process because energy is released. If the energy released when bonds form is greater than the energy needed to break bonds, the reaction is ___ overall.

question.hint: Energy in means one word; energy out means the other.
question.explanation: Bond breaking takes energy in (endothermic); bond making gives energy out (exothermic); more out than in means the overall reaction is exothermic.

activities.title: Investigating temperature changes (required practical)
activities.content:
## Which variables matter?

A typical investigation looks at how the temperature change of a neutralisation depends on the **volume of alkali** added to a fixed volume of acid.

**Method outline**

1. Measure 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid into a polystyrene cup standing in a beaker (for stability).
2. Record the starting temperature.
3. Add 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution, stir, and record the highest temperature reached.
4. Repeat, adding 5 cm³ more each time, up to about 40 cm³.
5. Plot temperature change against volume of alkali.

**What you see**

The temperature rises with each addition until all the acid is used up, then it falls because extra cold alkali is simply diluting the warm mixture. The peak shows the volume needed for exact neutralisation.

**Improving accuracy**

- Use a lid to reduce energy loss.
- Use a thermometer that reads to 0.5 °C or a digital probe.
- Repeat and take a mean.
- Stir so the temperature is even throughout the liquid.

question.text:
A student adds a spatula of ammonium nitrate to water in a polystyrene cup and stirs. The temperature falls from 21 °C to 12 °C.

(a) State whether the change is exothermic or endothermic, and explain how you know.

(b) Sketch or describe the reaction profile for this change, including the relative positions of reactants and products.

(c) Explain, in terms of bonds broken and bonds made, why the change is this type.

(d) Suggest one practical use for a reaction of this type.
question.hint: The temperature fell, so energy went from the water into the chemicals. Think about which side of the profile is higher, and which is bigger: energy to break bonds or energy released forming bonds.
question.explanation: (a) Endothermic, because the temperature of the surroundings (the water) decreased, showing energy was taken in. (b) The products are drawn at a higher energy level than the reactants, with an activation energy hump between them. (c) More energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants than is released when the new bonds form, so overall energy is absorbed. (d) Instant cold packs for sports injuries.

markScheme.criterion: Because the temperature decreased / energy was taken in from the surroundings
Products are at a higher energy level than the reactants on the profile
More energy needed to break bonds than is released when bonds are made

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Exothermic**: energy transferred **to** the surroundings, temperature **rises**. Combustion, neutralisation, oxidation, hand warmers.
- **Endothermic**: energy taken **in** from the surroundings, temperature **falls**. Thermal decomposition, citric acid + hydrogencarbonate, cold packs.
- **Reaction profile**: exothermic has products **below** reactants; endothermic has products **above**. The hump is the **activation energy**, measured from the reactants.
- A **catalyst** lowers the activation energy but leaves the overall energy change unchanged.
- **Breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds releases energy.**
- Higher: **energy change = bonds broken − bonds made**. Negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic. Count every bond, including those from big numbers in the equation.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: in an exothermic reaction the temperature of the surroundings increases.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so they warm up.

options.text: True

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is an endothermic process?
practiceQuestions.hint: Which one needs energy to keep going?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Thermal decomposition needs a continuous supply of heat; it stops if you stop heating. The other three all release energy.

burning a candle
magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid
options.feedback: This oxidation reaction gives out heat; the test tube gets warm.

metadata.blanksText: The ___ energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur. A ___ lowers this energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first word describes what gets the reaction 'activated'; the second is a substance that is not used up.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for reaction; a catalyst lowers it without being used up.

practiceQuestions.text: In a neutralisation experiment the temperature of the solution rises from 18.5 °C to 24.0 °C. Calculate the temperature change in °C.
practiceQuestions.hint: Subtract the start from the finish.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each feature of a reaction profile to what it represents.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about heights and differences on the graph.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The gap between reactant and product levels is the overall energy change; the hump measured from reactants is the activation energy; products drawn lower than reactants shows an exothermic reaction.

pairs.left: difference between reactant and product energy levels
height from reactants to the top of the hump

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. For the reaction H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr, the energy needed to break the bonds is 629 kJ and the energy released when the new bonds form is 732 kJ. Calculate the overall energy change in kJ/mol.
practiceQuestions.hint: Energy change = bonds broken − bonds made.

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. Calculate the energy change for the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ in kJ/mol. Bond energies: N≡N = 945, H–H = 436, N–H = 391 kJ/mol. Each NH₃ molecule contains three N–H bonds.
practiceQuestions.hint: Broken: one N≡N and three H–H. Made: six N–H bonds in total.

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. A bond energy calculation gives an energy change of +58 kJ/mol. What does this tell you?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A positive value means more energy is needed to break the bonds than is released forming the new ones, so the reaction is endothermic.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic; more energy is taken in breaking bonds than released making them.
The reaction is exothermic; more energy is released than taken in.
options.feedback: A negative value would indicate exothermic.

options.text: The reaction has no activation energy.
The reaction cannot happen.
options.feedback: Endothermic reactions do happen; they just need a supply of energy.

practiceQuestions.text: A student measures the temperature change when magnesium powder is added to copper sulfate solution in a glass beaker. Suggest two improvements to the apparatus that would give a more accurate value for the temperature change, and explain why each helps.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about where energy could be lost from the beaker.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Use a polystyrene cup instead of the glass beaker because it is a better insulator and reduces energy loss through the sides; add a lid to reduce energy loss from the surface (and hold the thermometer). Stirring or using a digital thermometer would also help.

markScheme.criterion: Use a polystyrene / insulated cup instead of glass
Reason: reduces energy / heat loss to the surroundings

practiceQuestions.text:
Hydrogen burns in oxygen in an exothermic reaction.

(a) Describe the reaction profile for this reaction, including the activation energy.

(b) Explain why the reaction does not start until a flame or spark is applied, even though it is exothermic.

(c) Explain, in terms of bonds, why the reaction is exothermic.
practiceQuestions.hint: Products lower than reactants. The hump has to be climbed first. Compare bonds broken with bonds made.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Products are at a lower energy than reactants; there is a hump (activation energy) between them, measured from the reactants to the peak. (b) Particles must have at least the activation energy to react; at room temperature too few collisions have enough energy, so a spark supplies the energy to break the first bonds. (c) The energy released forming the O–H bonds in water is greater than the energy needed to break the H–H and O=O bonds.

markScheme.criterion: Products are lower in energy than reactants (energy released)
Activation energy shown as the hump / from reactants to the peak
Particles need at least the activation energy to react; the spark provides this / few collisions have enough energy at room temperature
More energy released making O–H bonds than needed to break H–H and O=O bonds

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are endothermic changes? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Endothermic changes take energy in from the surroundings, so the surroundings get cooler or energy has to be supplied continuously.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Photosynthesis needs a constant input of light energy, and dissolving ammonium chloride makes the beaker feel cold because energy is taken in. A self-heating can and an iron-based hand warmer both release energy, so they are exothermic.

options.text: photosynthesis in a green leaf
dissolving ammonium chloride in water, which makes the beaker feel cold
a self-heating can that uses calcium oxide and water
options.feedback: The can gets hot because the reaction releases energy, so it is exothermic.

options.text: a disposable hand warmer in which iron powder oxidises
options.feedback: The warmer releases energy to your hands, so it is exothermic.

practiceQuestions.text: On a reaction profile the reactants are at 520 kJ, the peak of the curve is at 640 kJ and the products are at 410 kJ. Calculate the activation energy in kJ.
practiceQuestions.hint: Activation energy is the climb from the reactant level up to the top of the curve, not the difference between reactants and products.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Activation energy = peak − reactants = 640 − 520 = 120 kJ. (The overall change is 410 − 520 = −110 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic, but that is a separate quantity.)

practiceQuestions.text: A catalyst is added to an endothermic reaction. Which statement about the reaction profile is correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: A catalyst changes the route between reactants and products, not the reactants or products themselves.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so the peak of the curve is lower. The reactants and products are unchanged, so the products still sit above the reactants by the same amount and the reaction stays endothermic.

options.text: The peak of the curve is lower, but the products remain the same height above the reactants.
The reaction becomes exothermic because less energy is needed.
options.feedback: The overall energy change is fixed by the reactants and products, which the catalyst does not alter.

options.text: The reactants are raised to a higher energy level so they react more easily.
options.feedback: The energy of the reactants does not change; only the activation energy barrier is lowered.

options.text: The amount of energy taken in overall decreases.
options.feedback: The overall energy change is unchanged by a catalyst.

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. Calculate the energy change, in kJ/mol, for the complete combustion of methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies: C–H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O–H = 464 kJ/mol. Give a negative answer if the reaction is exothermic.
practiceQuestions.hint: Break four C–H bonds and two O=O bonds. Carbon dioxide has two C=O bonds, and each of the two water molecules has two O–H bonds.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bonds broken: (4 × 413) + (2 × 498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ. Bonds made: (2 × 805) + (4 × 464) = 1610 + 1856 = 3466 kJ. Energy change = 2648 − 3466 = −818 kJ/mol, so the reaction is exothermic.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about energy changes in reactions.

metadata.blanksText: In an ___ reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. In an ___ reaction energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature falls. The minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to start is called the ___ energy.

practiceQuestions.hint: Energy out and energy in have opposite names; the third answer is the height of the hump on a reaction profile.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exothermic reactions give out energy; endothermic reactions take it in; the activation energy is the minimum energy needed for particles to react.

practiceQuestions.text:
A student adds zinc powder to copper sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup and stirs. The temperature rises from 20 °C to 31 °C.

(a) State whether the change is exothermic or endothermic, and explain how you know.

(b) Describe the reaction profile for this change, including the relative positions of reactants and products.

(c) Explain, in terms of bonds broken and bonds made, why the change is this type.

(d) Suggest one practical use for a reaction of this type.
practiceQuestions.hint: The solution got warmer, so energy moved from the chemicals into the surroundings. Think about which side of the profile is lower, and whether more energy is released making bonds or used breaking them.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Exothermic, because the temperature of the surroundings (the solution) increased, showing energy was released. (b) The products are drawn at a lower energy level than the reactants, with an activation energy hump between them. (c) More energy is released when the new bonds form than is needed to break the bonds in the reactants, so overall energy is given out. (d) Hand warmers or self-heating food cans.

markScheme.criterion: Because the temperature increased / energy was released to the surroundings
Products are at a lower energy level than the reactants on the profile
More energy released when bonds are made than is needed to break bonds
Use: hand warmer / self-heating can / heating
